items.title: Less information, bigger deals
items.excerpt: Gartner found buyers swamped with good but contradictory information are 153% more likely to settle for something smaller than they planned. At Gilkes I opened on the emissions regulation, not the pump. Here's how to help a buyer make sense of what they've already got.
items.author: Scott Robinson
items.body:
89% of the B2B customers in a Gartner survey said the information they found while buying was high quality. That was the problem.

When there's too much of it and it contradicts itself, they're 153% more likely to settle for something smaller and less disruptive than they'd planned. Not a lost deal. A smaller one. And you'd never know, because an order still comes in.

## More information isn't helping your buyer

The figures come from a [Gartner press release in July 2019](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2019-07-29-gartner-reveals-new-b2b-sales-approach-to-win-in-toda) on a survey of more than 1,000 B2B customers. 89% said the information they came across during their purchase was high quality. Gartner says they were overwhelmed by the amount of trustworthy information, and by information that was often contradictory between suppliers. When that happened, they were 153% more likely to settle for a course of action smaller and less disruptive than originally planned.

Gartner says customers see sellers taking one of three approaches. Giving, where more is better and you send whatever's asked for. Telling, where the expert rep leans on their own experience and authority. And sense making, where the seller helps the customer prioritise sources, quantify trade offs and reconcile the information that conflicts, so they arrive at their own understanding. Gartner says 80% of the sellers who used sense making closed high quality, low regret deals.

A few caveats. It's a press release and the full report is for Gartner clients. The release describes B2B customers in general, not industrial buyers specifically, and it doesn't give the fieldwork dates. Gartner also runs a research and advice service for sales leaders, so read it as their finding, not a law. Still, if you're running a deal where engineering, procurement, finance and operations are all reading different things, it'll sound familiar.

## I opened on the regulation, not the pump

At GG&G, Gilkes in Kendal, we sold engine cooling pumps. I spotted a change in emissions regulation and realised the engine manufacturers were going to be forced to update their engines. New engine builds meant pumps had to be redesigned for them.

So I went round the engine manufacturers globally, or most of them, and I opened the conversation on the emissions regulations. Not on the product.

That bought us early access to the redesign work. Marine engines first, then rail, then some of the larger truck engines. The majority of our growth from £2.5M to £15.2M, up 508%, came from that.

The product wasn't cheap. It was built for the system and for the engine builder, and the value was in the technical expertise, the long life cycle and the quality compliance behind it. A spec sheet on its own would have been one more document on the pile. The regulation was something everybody in that engine programme had to deal with, and our pump was one answer inside it.

We took the cycle from 18 to 24 months down to around 12. That came from deal control, stakeholder mapping, relentless follow ups, face to face meetings and working directly with the technical teams. I've told the Caterpillar side of that story in [the three gates post](https://ringcraftcoaching.com/insights/technical-gets-you-in-procurement-decides).

Gartner didn't study what we did, and I'm not claiming their numbers explain it. But the shape is the same. We didn't add to the pile. We started from the problem they already had to solve.

## Sending everything is giving, not selling

When a buyer asks for everything, sending it feels like progress. That's the giving approach. Every datasheet lands next to somebody else's, and someone inside the buyer has to reconcile them. Gartner's finding is that when the information is too much and contradictory, the smaller, less disruptive option gets more likely.

Contradictory information also gives a buying group one more thing to disagree on. I've written about how [a buying group gets stuck on itself rather than on you](https://ringcraftcoaching.com/insights/agreement-is-the-deal). Your job is to make it easier for them to agree, not to give them more to read.

## What to do on a live deal this week

Take the biggest deal you've got open and do four things.

1. **Find the question they all have to answer.** Not your product. The thing driving the purchase: a regulation, a shutdown, a budget cycle, a failure they can't have again. Open your next conversation on that.
2. **Cut your next send to one page.** What they need to decide, the two or three trade offs that matter, and where your information and a competitor's disagree, and why.
3. **Ask what's confusing them.** "What are your people getting different answers on?" Whatever comes back is where you're needed.
4. **Ask what decision a request is for before you answer it.** Then send the piece that helps with that decision, not the whole folder.

## The short version

Your buyer isn't short of good information. Gartner's 2019 survey says too much of it, especially when it contradicts, makes them 153% more likely to settle for something smaller and less disruptive than planned. At Gilkes I opened on the emissions regulation, not the pump, and the majority of a 508% increase came from that. Help the buyer make sense of what they've already got before you add to it.

If you've got a deal that's shrinking or stuck while the buyer reads, bring it to a [free Stalled Deal Review](https://ringcraftcoaching.com/stalled-deal-review/). Thirty minutes on one stalled deal: where it has actually stopped and the three things to do next.

## Sources

- Gartner, "Gartner Reveals New B2B Sales Approach to Win in Today's Information Age", 2019. https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2019-07-29-gartner-reveals-new-b2b-sales-approach-to-win-in-toda

items.title: Selected, approved, then voted down
items.excerpt: Switzerland picked the Gripen, a law was passed for it, and voters still turned it down. A selection isn't a signature. Here's how to find everyone who can still stop your deal after the yes.
items.author: Scott Robinson
items.body:
Switzerland picked its new fighter jet in November 2011. Saab won a three way contest, the contract was awarded and a law was passed for the purchase. On 18 May 2014, 53.4% of Swiss voters rejected it.

Saab hadn't lost to Dassault or the Eurofighter. It had already beaten both. The last word sat with people who were never part of the evaluation.

## Selected isn't signed

[Bloomberg's report, republished by swissinfo.ch in 2014](https://www.swissinfo.ch/eng/swiss-reject-3-5-billion-gripen-purchase-in-blow-to-saab/38607010), sets out how it happened. Opponents collected the 50,000 signatures needed to force a national referendum to cancel the law. They argued the planes would cost 10 billion francs over their lifetime, money that could be spent elsewhere. Voters rejected the 3.1 billion franc order for 22 Gripens, and Saab's Lennart Sindahl had already said that if voters said no, he couldn't see a reworked Swiss deal happening.

One caveat. It's a press report, and it says nothing about what Saab did or didn't do to win the public over. So this isn't a story about Saab getting it wrong. It's a story about where the decision actually sat. The defence ministry had started the purchase and a law had been passed. The one group that could still say no had a vote of its own.

And it wasn't hidden. The same report says the latest survey before the vote showed some 51 percent opposed, and a Swedbank analyst called the result "not exactly unexpected given the opinion polls".

## I lost one with the same shape

Mine was smaller and a lot earlier. At Ford, I had a managing director who wanted to change his entire fleet. Priced, specified, agreed. It never moved.

I'd been taught to sell to the man who signs the cheque, and I did. His service team, his finance people and his management all had their own reasons to stay where they were, and he was never going to make his own staff unhappy to please me. Nobody beat me on that deal. I lost it on my own. I've written up [the full Ford story](https://ringcraftcoaching.com/insights/the-deal-i-lost-on-my-own) if you want the detail.

The Swiss vote and that fleet deal are the same thing at very different sizes. The person who said yes was real. They just weren't the last word.

## A yes can be reopened

The US Air Force's new tanker competition shows another way a won deal comes undone. The Air Force selected Northrop Grumman on 29 February 2008 and Boeing filed a protest on 11 March. In June the [US Government Accountability Office sustained it](https://www.gao.gov/assets/a120582.html), finding "a number of significant errors that could have affected the outcome of what was a close competition".

One of those errors is worth reading twice. The Air Force told Boeing it had fully met an objective on operational utility, later decided it hadn't, and didn't tell Boeing. GAO said that was improper and recommended reopening discussions, getting revised proposals and making a new selection. GAO also said it saw no evidence of intentional wrongdoing and that its decision took no view on the merits of either tanker.

Boeing won the rerun. [NPR reported in February 2011](https://www.wbez.org/news/2011/02/24/usaf-picks-boeing-to-build-tankers-35-billion-contract) that the Air Force had awarded Boeing the contract, and that Pentagon officials said both bidders had met all minimum requirements. The report doesn't say why Boeing won the second time.

Bid protests belong to public procurement, so most sellers will never file one. The lesson I take from it travels anyway. Know the buyer's stated rules in detail, and keep in writing what the buyer tells you about where you stand.

## What to do on a live deal this week

Pick the deal in your pipeline that's furthest along. Selected, preferred supplier, verbal yes, whatever your version is. Then do three things.

1. **Write the after yes list.** Every person or group who can still stop it once your contact says yes: finance, the users, the service team, legal, a board, a parent company. Next to each one, write what they lose if it goes ahead.
2. **Ask your champion one question.** "Once you've said yes, what has to happen before an order is raised, and who's involved at each step?" If they can't answer it, you've found where the deal is going to stop.
3. **Put their words in writing.** When the buyer tells you where you stand, send a short recap that day. It keeps everyone honest, including you.

If a name on that list has never heard from you, that's this week's work. I've written more on [the people who can veto you and never take your call](https://ringcraftcoaching.com/insights/the-people-who-can-veto-you).

## The short version

A selection isn't a signature. Saab won the contest and a law was passed, and voters still said no. Boeing lost, then reopened the decision through the buyer's own rules and won the rerun. I had a managing director's yes at Ford and still lost the fleet. Find everyone who can still say no after the yes, and get to them before they get their say.

If you've got a deal that's been selected and hasn't moved since, bring it to a [free Stalled Deal Review](https://ringcraftcoaching.com/stalled-deal-review/). Thirty minutes on one stalled deal: where it has actually stopped and the three things to do next.

## Sources

- Bloomberg via SWI swissinfo.ch, "Swiss Reject $3.5 Billion Gripen Purchase in Blow to Saab", 2014. https://www.swissinfo.ch/eng/swiss-reject-3-5-billion-gripen-purchase-in-blow-to-saab/38607010
- US Government Accountability Office, "Air Force Procurement: Aerial Refueling Tanker Protest (GAO-08-991T)", 2008. https://www.gao.gov/assets/a120582.html
- NPR via WBEZ Chicago, "USAF Picks Boeing To Build Tankers; $35 Billion Contract", 2011. https://www.wbez.org/news/2011/02/24/usaf-picks-boeing-to-build-tankers-35-billion-contract

items.title: Your buyer isn't stuck on you. They're stuck on each other.
items.excerpt: Most of the buying teams in a Gartner survey showed unhealthy conflict during the decision. On a deal with several people in it, the fight usually isn't with you. Here's how I got a buying committee in Raufoss to agree with itself, and why I ran technical and commercial in parallel on Saab.
items.author: Scott Robinson
items.body:
Seventy four percent. That's the share of B2B buying teams Gartner found showing unhealthy conflict during the buying decision.

Your deal might not be stuck because they don't want it. It might be stuck because they haven't agreed with each other yet.

## The fight usually isn't with you

In a press release in May 2025, Gartner reported that [seventy four percent of B2B buyer teams demonstrate unhealthy conflict](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2025-05-07-gartner-sales-survey-finds-74-percent-of-b2b-buyer-teams-demonstrate-unhealthy-conflict-during-the-decision-process) during the buying decision, according to a Gartner survey. The same release describes a survey of 632 B2B buyers run in August and September 2024. Gartner defines unhealthy conflict as members having conflicting objectives, disagreeing on the best course of action, or being overruled by external decision makers.

It's easy to treat a stalled deal as a problem between you and your contact. Chase harder, send another proposal, offer a bit off. None of that helps if the people on the other side of the table can't agree on what they're buying, or why.

The same survey found buying groups that reach consensus are [2.5 times more likely to report that their deal was high quality](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2025-05-07-gartner-sales-survey-finds-74-percent-of-b2b-buyer-teams-demonstrate-unhealthy-conflict-during-the-decision-process). Be clear on what you're looking at. It's the buyer's own view of the deal, not a seller's win rate. But it tells you where to point your effort.

Gartner's Delainey Kirkwood [put these groups at five to 16 people](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2025-05-07-gartner-sales-survey-finds-74-percent-of-b2b-buyer-teams-demonstrate-unhealthy-conflict-during-the-decision-process) across as many as four functions. That's one firm's range, not a fixed size, and your deal might have more or fewer. If you want to know who sits in that group and never takes your call, I wrote about [the people who can veto you](https://ringcraftcoaching.com/insights/the-people-who-can-veto-you).

## What I did on Saab

The $650K naval contract I won with Saab in Sweden, while I was at Lansmont, came through a multi stage tender. Technical qualification and commercial negotiation ran at the same time.

I ran both in parallel rather than finishing one and starting the other. And I kept the engagement going with the people making the decision across every stage, not just at each gate. My view is simple: a supplier who goes quiet between gates gets forgotten by the time the next one opens.

Think about what happens when you don't. The technical people sign you off in March. Commercial first properly look at you in June. Now you've got two groups forming two opinions at two different times, and the second group doesn't care how hard the first one worked. Running them side by side keeps both looking at the same supplier, at the same time.

That contract opened Scandinavian defence and government markets the business hadn't been in before. The gates themselves are a separate fight, and I've written about why [technical gets you in and procurement decides](https://ringcraftcoaching.com/insights/technical-gets-you-in-procurement-decides).

## Give the group one thing to agree on

The £500,000 order I closed this year with a defence contractor in Raufoss, Norway, worked the same way. The decision sat with a buying committee, and everyone on it had to be aligned.

One thing came up time and time again: their schedule, and the date they needed to start. So I worked backwards from that date, confirmed with the client that it couldn't move, and presented a drop dead date for the order. I didn't sell the committee my priorities. I built the order around the one thing they kept raising themselves.

Gartner's survey has a number on this. Tailoring for buying group relevance [positively impacts consensus by 20%](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2025-05-07-gartner-sales-survey-finds-74-percent-of-b2b-buyer-teams-demonstrate-unhealthy-conflict-during-the-decision-process). Content that focuses on individual level relevance had a [59% negative impact](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2025-05-07-gartner-sales-survey-finds-74-percent-of-b2b-buyer-teams-demonstrate-unhealthy-conflict-during-the-decision-process) on buying group consensus.

That second figure should make you stop. A separate pack for every person, the technical file for the engineer and a savings sheet for finance, feels like good selling. On Gartner's numbers it can push each person further into their own corner.

## What to do on a live deal this week

1. Write down every person who has to agree, and next to each name what they need from this decision.
2. Find the one thing they all share. A date, a shutdown, a budget line, a regulation. Get the customer to confirm it won't move.
3. Rewrite your next document around that shared thing, not your contact's priorities. One document the whole group reads.
4. Run the technical and commercial conversations side by side. Don't let one wait for the other.
5. Ask your contact one question: "Who in the group isn't convinced yet, and what would they need to see?"

## The short version

Gartner reported that 74% of B2B buyer teams show unhealthy conflict, and in its survey of 632 buyers, groups that reached consensus were 2.5 times more likely to call their deal high quality. Stop selling to one person's priorities. Find the thing the whole group already cares about, build around it, and keep every side moving at the same time.

If you've got a deal where everyone says they like it and nothing moves, bring it to a [Stalled Deal Review](https://ringcraftcoaching.com/stalled-deal-review/). It's free. Thirty minutes on one stalled deal: where it has actually stopped and the three things to do next.

## Sources

- Gartner, "Gartner Sales Survey Finds 74% of B2B Buyer Teams Demonstrate Unhealthy Conflict During The Decision Process", 2025. https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2025-05-07-gartner-sales-survey-finds-74-percent-of-b2b-buyer-teams-demonstrate-unhealthy-conflict-during-the-decision-process

items.title: One order, six businesses in the chain. I worked all six.
items.excerpt: Gartner, CEB and Forrester all count buying groups differently, and none of them describes a decision getting simpler. How I worked every business in the chain on a £150,000 order for 22 Bishopsgate, and what to check on your own deal this week.
items.author: Scott Robinson
items.body:
One order for pressure gauges and thermometers on 22 Bishopsgate. Two developers, a consultant, a main contractor, an MEP contractor and a supplier in the chain. By the time I asked for the order, I already knew we had it.

It landed around August 2019, worth around £150,000, for Brannan. It didn't land because I found the one person who signs. It landed because I worked every business in that chain.

## The number depends on who counted

There's no single answer to how many people sit in a buying decision. It depends who counted and what they counted.

In 2016, CEB wrote in [The Revolution in B2B Buying](https://www.multivu.com/players/English/7427254-ceb-challenge-align-prescribe-b2b-sales-strategy/docs/the-revolution-in-b2b-buying-%E2%80%93-how-leading-companies-overcome-the-complexities-of-customer-buying-1945904544.pdf) that its initial research found 5.4 stakeholders involved in each B2B purchase on average, and that the number had risen to 6.8, representing 3.7 different functions. CEB's own conclusion was that large, diverse buying groups struggle to agree, resulting in dysfunction and indecision. That's ten year old data, so read it as history, not as today.

In May 2025, Gartner released [a survey of 632 B2B buyers](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2025-05-07-gartner-sales-survey-finds-74-percent-of-b2b-buyer-teams-demonstrate-unhealthy-conflict-during-the-decision-process), run in August and September 2024. In that release, Gartner's Delainey Kirkwood said buying groups range from five to 16 people across as many as four functions, and that each member may have differing priorities and opinions.

In January 2026, [Forrester's release on The State Of Business Buying, 2026](https://www.forrester.com/press-newsroom/forrester-2026-the-state-of-business-buying/) said the typical buying decision now includes 13 internal stakeholders and nine external influencers, with that number rising for more complex or strategic purchases. The release doesn't give the method, and the external influencers aren't the internal group, so don't add them together.

None of the three pages says which industries were covered, so don't read any of them as industrial data. And they don't agree with each other. CEB showed a rise from 5.4 to 6.8. Forrester's release says buying groups are growing larger. Gartner's says they're more diverse than ever. Different words, but none of them describes a decision getting simpler.

## Who actually pays for the extra names

This bit is easy to miss. The same Forrester release says 94% of buyers with groups of six or more report clear benefits, including a better ability to secure budget and a greater likelihood of approval. A big group isn't bad news for the buyer.

The cost lands on the seller who only knows one of them. Every name you haven't spoken to is a set of priorities being argued without you. I've written before about [the people who can veto you and never take your call](https://ringcraftcoaching.com/insights/the-people-who-can-veto-you). The more names in the decision, the more of those there are.

## Bishopsgate, one business at a time

22 Bishopsgate is a huge tower in London. The initial decision to specify Brannan came from WSP, the consultant. That was the start, not the finish.

Multiplex, the main contractor, then had to have the confidence to use our product. Being a UK manufacturer that had been going for more than 100 years helped in that conversation. Hotchkiss, the MEP contractor, had to go with Wolseley, our partner, because Wolseley had the relationship. So I made sure Wolseley kept me in the conversation. And above all of them sat the developers, AXA among them.

I held meetings to understand the buying process. I talked to the contractor to make sure we had product ready when it was needed on site. I worked every business and every contact in my lane, and made sure each of them knew who Brannan was.

When I finally asked for the order, I already knew we had it, because multiple people upstream had said they were using Brannan products. I'd closed it before I had to ask.

## What to do on a live deal this week

1. Write down every business in the chain, not just every person at your customer. Developer, consultant, main contractor, subcontractor, distributor, end user. Whatever your version of that list is.
2. Next to each one, write the name of the person there you've actually spoken to. Every blank is a conversation happening without you.
3. Next to each name, write what that business needs before it'll back you. On Bishopsgate, Multiplex needed confidence in the product and Hotchkiss had to go with Wolseley, who had the relationship. Yours will be different.
4. Ask your contact one question: "Who else will want a say before this is signed?" Then ask to meet them.
5. Before you ask for the order, count how many people upstream have told you they're using you. If the answer is one, you've got more work to do first.

## The short version

More names in the decision isn't the problem. In Forrester's research, 94% of buyers with groups of six or more report clear benefits. The problem is every name you haven't spoken to. On Bishopsgate there were six businesses in the chain, and I made sure every one of them knew who we were before I asked.

Got a deal where you only really know one name? [Bring a stalled deal](https://ringcraftcoaching.com/stalled-deal-review/). The free Stalled Deal Review is thirty minutes on one stalled deal, and you leave knowing where it's actually stopped and the three things to do next. If you want someone in your corner on the deals after that, that's what [Ringcraft](https://ringcraftcoaching.com/) is for.

## Sources

- CEB, "The Revolution in B2B Buying", 2016. https://www.multivu.com/players/English/7427254-ceb-challenge-align-prescribe-b2b-sales-strategy/docs/the-revolution-in-b2b-buying-%E2%80%93-how-leading-companies-overcome-the-complexities-of-customer-buying-1945904544.pdf
- Gartner, "Gartner Sales Survey Finds 74% of B2B Buyer Teams Demonstrate Unhealthy Conflict During The Decision Process", 2025. https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2025-05-07-gartner-sales-survey-finds-74-percent-of-b2b-buyer-teams-demonstrate-unhealthy-conflict-during-the-decision-process
- Forrester, "Forrester's 2026 Buyer Insights: GenAI Is Upending B2B Buying As Leaders Face Mounting Pressure To Justify Every Dollar Spent", 2026. https://www.forrester.com/press-newsroom/forrester-2026-the-state-of-business-buying/

items.title: The people who can veto you and never take your call
items.excerpt: Research from LinkedIn and Bain says hidden buyers in procurement, finance, legal and operations vetoed around half the vendors on the shortlist. How I worked one date with a buying committee in Norway on a £500,000 order, and what to check on your own deal this week.
items.author: Scott Robinson
items.body:
71% of hidden buyers say they have little or no interaction with sales teams. They're the people who can derail your deal.

That figure comes from [a 2025 report by Edelman and LinkedIn](https://www.edelman.com/insights/hidden-buyer-b2b). Their hidden buyers are the people in finance, legal, compliance, procurement and operations who may never use your product or sign the contract, and still have real power over whether you win it. It's written by Edelman's business marketing chair to make the case for thought leadership, so read the framing with that in mind, and the article doesn't give the sample. The point still stands. The people who can stop your order are mostly people you've had little or no contact with.

## What the research says they do

[The Hidden Buyer Gap](https://business.linkedin.com/advertise/resources/b2b-institute/b2b-research/trends/the-hidden-buyer-gap), by Jann Martin Schwarz and Mimi Turner of LinkedIn, published by the LinkedIn B2B Institute, comes from research on enterprise buying groups co authored with Bain & Company. The page isn't dated but carries a 2025 copyright. Almost all of their sample said the product experts shortlisted between two and five vendors after technical testing. Then the hidden buyers vetoed around half the vendors on that shortlist, because they didn't satisfy their risk mitigation criteria.

Read it with the caveats on. There's no sample size or date on the page, it sits on LinkedIn's advertising site and argues that marketers should reach these people, and it doesn't say which industries were studied. Don't read it as industrial data. Treat it as a direction, not a measurement. But if you've ever had the engineer on side and still not got the order, the direction will feel familiar.

## A buying committee in Norway

In January 2026 our partner told me about a requirement at a defence contractor in Raufoss, Norway. I was International Sales Director at Lansmont. They needed an upgrade to a testing machine, and the deal ran through the partner.

I got the spec and there was customisation to work on. At that point I had direct contact with the end user. From them I found out two things: when they needed to complete testing, and how the buying process actually worked inside the business.

The decision sat with a buying committee, and they needed to get everyone aligned. The one thing that came up time and time again was the testing schedule and when they needed to start.

So I worked backwards from that schedule, confirmed with the client that there was no movement on it, and presented a drop dead date for the order. I supplied what they needed to get the approvals, and I used the lead time as leverage to quicken the process up.

What nearly lost it was our own lead time. The parts are major cast items for the machine and have to be ordered. I worked with the US team, nailed down the delivery schedule on parts and made sure there was time to hit the milestones. Then I presented the situation and made the client realise the issues missing the drop dead date would cause.

There was some back and forth, and the negotiating took a month. Daily follow up phone calls, no missed dates. The order dropped on time for their delivery schedule. £500,000, closed in 2026.

## Why the date did the work

A committee doesn't agree on your product. The LinkedIn piece says hidden buyers judge vendors on risk mitigation, compliance, financial stability and reputation, not product performance. That's a different conversation for every person in the room.

The testing schedule was the one thing that came up time and time again. Once it was fixed, with no movement on it, the drop dead date for the order followed straight from it. I'd already supplied what they needed to get the approvals.

I've been on the wrong side of this too. Early in my career at Ford I had a managing director who wanted to change his entire fleet. I'd been taught to sell to the man who signs the cheque, and [the service team, finance and management all had their own reasons to stay where they were](https://ringcraftcoaching.com/insights/the-deal-i-lost-on-my-own). It never moved.

## What to do on a live deal this week

1. Ask your contact one question: "Who else has to approve this before an order can be placed, and what does each of them need to see?" Write the names down.
2. Next to each name, write what they're protecting. Budget, contract terms, compliance, the operation running. If you can't fill it in, that's your gap.
3. Find the date the customer can't move. Not your quarter end, theirs. Confirm with them that there's no movement on it.
4. Check your own side against that date. Lead times, approvals, anything that has to be ordered. Mine nearly cost me the deal.
5. Give your contact what each approver needs, in their terms, so they can carry it into the rooms you won't be in.

## The short version

The people who can veto you mostly won't take your call, and the research says they're judging risk, not your product. Find out who they are, what each of them needs, and the one date the whole committee cares about.

Got a deal that's sitting with people you've never met? [Bring a stalled deal](https://ringcraftcoaching.com/stalled-deal-review/). The free Stalled Deal Review is thirty minutes on one stalled deal, and you leave knowing where it's actually stopped and the three things to do next.

## Sources

- Edelman, "The Rise of the Hidden Buyer: Rethinking B2B Influence Beyond the Obvious", 2025. https://www.edelman.com/insights/hidden-buyer-b2b
- LinkedIn B2B Institute, "The Hidden Buyer Gap", undated (page copyright 2025). https://business.linkedin.com/advertise/resources/b2b-institute/b2b-research/trends/the-hidden-buyer-gap

items.title: Fifteen years in the ADNOC and Aramco specs. Somebody still had to sell it.
items.excerpt: Being specified is the biggest lever on a project. It is not the job. What I actually did to take Middle East sales up 167% in a year, what happened on 22 Bishopsgate, and five questions to ask before you walk away.
items.author: Scott Robinson
items.body:
Hughes were written into the ADNOC and Aramco specifications fifteen years before I joined. In 2024 I took Middle East sales up 167% on the year before.

I did not do that by getting into a specification. They were already in it.

Being specified is the single biggest lever in project sales. It tilts the odds hard in your favour and I would always rather be in than out. But a specification is a position, not an order. I am not going to tell you a story about those fifteen years, because I was not there. I can tell you what I did.

## What 167% actually took

I spent nine months out of twelve in the GCC that year. It was not a campaign. It was presence.

I removed the distributors that were no longer fit for purpose. The incumbent was a PPE distributor selling safety equipment, and that is a completely different sale. I spotted that the fire safety sector aligned far better and built a strong relationship there.

I got close to the EPC contractors in the region: Técnicas Reunidas, Samsung, Saipem, McDermott, Wood, CNPC, Tecnimont, Target Engineering.

Then I ran two prongs. Direct where we could, and bidding alongside the fire safety players where we could not. That mapped the market properly, and it opened up projects the business was never even getting to pitch for while it ran purely through distribution.

The reason matters. In a [2018 McKinsey survey of more than 100 senior US manufacturing executives](https://www.mckinsey.com/industries/industrials/our-insights/the-coming-shakeout-in-industrial-distribution), manufacturers aiming for more direct sales gave developing more end customer relationships as their top reason, at 40% of respondents. Capturing the distributors' margins came in at 14%. That is US manufacturers in 2018, so read it with that in mind, but it is the right order of priorities. The relationship with the end customer comes first.

> Being written in gives you a position. Somebody still has to go and sell from it.

## Specified is where the work starts

22 Bishopsgate is a huge London tower. I was at Brannan, and the decision to specify our gauges and thermometers came from WSP. Job done, you would think.

It was not. We then had to give Multiplex, the main contractor, the confidence to use us. Hotchkiss, the MEP contractor, had to go with Wolseley, our partner, who held the relationship. So I worked with every business in the chain, the developers, WSP, Multiplex, Hotchkiss and Wolseley, and made sure every one of them knew who Brannan was.

I closed it before I had to ask for the business. When I did ask, I already knew we had it, because several people upstream had told me they were using us. Around £150,000, landed around August 2019.

## If you are outside it

It is not pass or fail. Thousands of projects are won by manufacturers who are on the approved vendor list and not written into the specification. It depends on the EPC, the operator, the budget and the commercial case.

Treat being outside the spec as the end of the job and you either walk away from winnable business or spend six months pushing at the wrong door.

On Marjan I booked a call with Aramco and mapped the timings from the owner's side. Nobody else did it, because everybody else was working the EPC. That is why [both angles](https://ringcraftcoaching.com/#method) is part of the method. The contractor will tell you what the specification says. The owner can tell you what they actually want and when they actually want it.

## Five questions before you walk away

1. Are you on the approved vendor list, or could you be in the time available?
2. Which EPC holds this, and how much room do they have?
3. What does the operator actually care about on this job?
4. Is there budget, and whose is it?
5. What is the commercial case for changing, stated in terms somebody can defend in a meeting you will not be in?

Some of the time those answers tell you to leave it alone, and that is a good result if you get it in a fortnight rather than a year.

## The short version

In the spec, go and sell from it. Out of it, find out before you walk. Either way, work every name in the chain.

Outside the spec on one right now? [Bring a stalled deal](https://ringcraftcoaching.com/stalled-deal-review/). Thirty minutes on one deal, no charge, and you leave knowing where it has actually stopped and the three things to do next.

## Sources

- McKinsey, "The coming shakeout in industrial distribution", 2019. https://www.mckinsey.com/industries/industrials/our-insights/the-coming-shakeout-in-industrial-distribution

items.title: We pushed into Caterpillar's engine build. They asked for an open book review.
items.excerpt: Technical gets you into the build. Quality decides whether you stay in it. Procurement decides whether you get paid. What that looked like at Caterpillar, GE and Saab, and how I run the gates side by side.
items.author: Scott Robinson
items.body:
I pushed to get into Caterpillar's engine build programme, and they asked for an open book review of our supply chain.

That is how you find out how many gates there are.

Technical gets you into the engine build. Quality decides whether you stay in it. Procurement decides whether you get paid. Win the first and lose either of the other two and you have worked eighteen months for nothing.

## What the gates look like on a real deal

I was at GG&G, Gilbert Gilkes & Gordon in Kendal, selling engine cooling pumps. Over the time I was there the business went from £2.5M to £15.2M, and the cycle came down from 18 to 24 months to around 12.

We started with Caterpillar's technical people, on marine engines. That was the easy part to enjoy. An engineer wants to talk about the product. You want to talk about the product. You can go home thinking it is going well.

Then the open book request landed. I pushed back. Eventually I yielded, but I presented it in a format that suited us. And behind that sat quality gateway after quality gateway, which was normal across most of our customers.

GE was the other side of the same coin. They sold few marine engines a year, big and low volume, so we wanted to charge for the design work. Around £150,000. I closed it. It was the first time in Gilkes' very long history that they had charged for pump design work. That was a commercial conversation, and technical could not have had it for me.

## Procurement is not waiting at the end

[Forrester's 2026 report on business buying](https://www.forrester.com/press-newsroom/forrester-2026-the-state-of-business-buying/) says procurement professionals are decision makers in 53% of buying cycles and engage from the start of the process. That comes from a press release that does not state the sample or break it down by industry, so treat it as a direction rather than a measurement.

The same release puts the typical decision at 13 internal stakeholders and nine external influencers. [Delainey Kirkwood of Gartner, in a May 2025 release](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2025-05-07-gartner-sales-survey-finds-74-percent-of-b2b-buyer-teams-demonstrate-unhealthy-conflict-during-the-decision-process), says five to 16 people across as many as four functions. Forrester lists outside influencers separately and that Gartner release does not say whether its figure includes them, so there is no single right number. The point is that it is a lot more people than the engineer you were talking to.

## Do not wait for the next gate

On Saab's naval programme in Sweden, a $650K multi stage tender, technical qualification and commercial negotiation ran at the same time. I ran them in parallel and stayed in front of the procurement decision makers at every stage rather than waiting for the next gate.

> Sequence is how sellers lose eighteen months. Run the gates side by side.

Treat them as three separate sales inside one deal. That is what [the decision map](https://ringcraftcoaching.com/#method) is for. Put a name against each gate this week, and ask each one a different question.

**Technical.** What do you need to see before you will put your name to it? Get the list in writing and agree it is the whole list.

**Quality.** What would make you take us out? Ask it while things are going well, and put your own quality person in front of theirs.

**Procurement.** What do you need in order to justify this? Not the discount. The justification. Then give it to them in their terms: total cost, risk and what a delay costs.

If you can only name the person at one of those gates, you know where to spend next week.

## The short version

Win all three gates or you have not won. Start all three early, and never let the engineer be your only friend in the building.

Got one that has stopped at a gate? [Bring a stalled deal](https://ringcraftcoaching.com/stalled-deal-review/). Thirty minutes on one deal, no charge, and you leave knowing where it has actually stopped and the three things to do next.

## Sources

- Forrester, "Forrester's 2026 Buyer Insights: GenAI Is Upending B2B Buying As Leaders Face Mounting Pressure To Justify Every Dollar Spent", 2026. https://www.forrester.com/press-newsroom/forrester-2026-the-state-of-business-buying/
- Gartner, "Gartner Sales Survey Finds 74% of B2B Buyer Teams Demonstrate Unhealthy Conflict During The Decision Process", 2025. https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2025-05-07-gartner-sales-survey-finds-74-percent-of-b2b-buyer-teams-demonstrate-unhealthy-conflict-during-the-decision-process

items.title: He said yes. He signs the cheques. It still never happened.
items.excerpt: A managing director agreed to change his entire fleet and nobody beat me to it. Twenty years later a £1.9M Aramco package started going the same way. What I did differently, and what I do on any deal that goes quiet.
items.author: Scott Robinson
items.body:
A managing director told me he wanted to change his entire fleet. Priced, specified, agreed. It never happened, and nobody beat me to it.

I was early in my career at Ford, selling contract hire. I had been taught to sell to the man who signs the cheque, so that is exactly what I did. His service team, his finance people and his management all had their own reasons to stay where they were. He was never going to make his own staff unhappy to please me.

Nobody beat me on that deal. I lost it on my own.

## It is not a rare way to lose

In a [2022 Harvard Business Review article](https://hbr.org/2022/06/stop-losing-sales-to-customer-indecision), Matthew Dixon and Ted McKenna report on more than 2.5 million recorded sales conversations. Between 40% and 60% of deals ended up lost to customers who expressed their intent to purchase and then failed to act. The study spans transactional and complex sales across the board rather than industrial sales in particular, and it comes from the authors' own book on the subject, so read it with that in mind.

Gartner asked buyers what goes on inside their buying groups. In a [survey of 632 B2B buyers, published in May 2025](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2025-05-07-gartner-sales-survey-finds-74-percent-of-b2b-buyer-teams-demonstrate-unhealthy-conflict-during-the-decision-process), 74% of buyer teams demonstrated unhealthy conflict during the decision. That is buyers reporting on themselves. In the same May 2025 release, Delainey Kirkwood of Gartner puts those groups at five to 16 people across as many as four functions.

That is the argument you are not in. It happens while you are sat at your desk waiting for an answer.

## Twenty years later, the same deal

Marjan Package 9. £1.9M, through Técnicas Reunidas, for Saudi Aramco. I inherited it late, after a sales restructure. Technical was signed off. The documentation was agreed. The terms were sat there going nowhere.

Same thing as the fleet deal. It looked done and it was not moving.

The difference was that by then I knew whose room the decision was actually in. So I stopped guessing at it through the contractor. I booked a call with Aramco and mapped the timings from the owner's side. Nobody else did that, because everybody else was working the EPC.

> Once I had the date the operator needed units on site, the deal had a spine.

I worked the lead time backwards from that date with Borja at Técnicas Reunidas. I ran the bonds and the legal in parallel instead of one after the other. It closed on the operator's on site date. Around 190 units.

I did not push harder than the Ford deal. I went and found out who the decision belonged to and what they actually needed.

## What to do on yours this week

Pick the one deal that has gone quiet and answer these on paper. This is [the decision map](https://ringcraftcoaching.com/#method) in its simplest form.

1. **Where does the decision actually live?** Not who signs. Who has to be comfortable before anybody signs. Write the names down. A question mark counts as an answer, and it tells you where to go next.
2. **Who is arguing against you, and what is their reason?** Most of the reasons belong to the business, not the person in front of you. Ask your contact who would be happiest if this never happened.
3. **What is in your champion's hands?** They are having that argument without you. Write them one page that answers the objections they will get.
4. **What is the real date?** Get it from the people who need the thing, not the people passing it on. Then work backwards through your lead time and show them the last day they can order.

If you cannot answer those, the deal has not stalled. You have lost sight of it.

## The short version

The man who signs is rarely the man who decides. Find the room, find who is arguing, and get the real date from the owner.

Got one that has stopped? [Bring a stalled deal](https://ringcraftcoaching.com/stalled-deal-review/). Thirty minutes on one deal, no charge, and you leave knowing where it has actually stopped and the three things to do next.

## Sources

- Harvard Business Review, "Stop Losing Sales to Customer Indecision", 2022. https://hbr.org/2022/06/stop-losing-sales-to-customer-indecision
- Gartner, "Gartner Sales Survey Finds 74% of B2B Buyer Teams Demonstrate Unhealthy Conflict During The Decision Process", 2025. https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2025-05-07-gartner-sales-survey-finds-74-percent-of-b2b-buyer-teams-demonstrate-unhealthy-conflict-during-the-decision-process
